effect_estimate.comment: Note slight rounding differences in the paper between Abstract (overall 47%, 95% CI: 45%-49%; range 18% [95% CI: 14%-23%] to 76% [95% CI: 70%-81%]) and Results/Table 1 (overall 47%, 95% CI: 44%-49%, weighted 46.7%; range 19% [95% CI: 15%-24%] in Lukanga WSC to 77% [95% CI: 71%-82%] in Kafubu WSC), and p-value thresholds between text p. 14 and Table 4 footnotes on p. 15.
effect_estimate.value: Overall, 47% (95% CI: 44%, 49%; unweighted n = 1,398/3,047) of urban/peri-urban piped-water households reported water being unavailable for >=1 full day in the preceding fortnight, varying across regulated provider coverage areas (PCAs) from 19% (95% CI: 15%, 24%) in Lukanga WSC to 77% (95% CI: 71%, 82%) in Kafubu WSC. In two-level multilevel logistic regression (n = 3,047 households in 177 clusters), home ownership (at least partly owning vs not owning) was associated with higher odds of interruption in Model 1 (OR = 1.31, SE = 0.13, p < 0.01) and Model 2 (OR = 1.32, SE = 0.13, p < 0.01). Controlling for household factors (Model 1, ref: Lusaka WSC), interruption odds differed markedly across utility service areas: Kafubu WSC OR = 8.02 (SE = 3.40, p < 0.01), Mulongo WSC OR = 3.77 (SE = 1.85, p < 0.05), Luapula WSC OR = 2.89 (SE = 1.45, p < 0.05), Chambeshi WSC OR = 2.43 (SE = 0.94, p < 0.05), Nkana WSC OR = 2.24 (SE = 0.90, p < 0.10), and Lukanga WSC OR = 0.36 (SE = 0.15, p < 0.05). Using a neighbour's tap vs piped into dwelling had OR = 1.33 (SE = 0.21, p < 0.10) in Model 2. At provider level (Model 2), GDP per capita reduced interruption odds (OR = 0.51 per $1,000, SE = 0.11, p < 0.01), while regulator-reported LPCD had no main effect (OR = 1.01, SE = 0.01, NS) but interacted with middle neighbourhood wealth (OR = 0.97, SE = 0.01, p < 0.05) and provider GDP per capita (OR = 1.02, SE = 0.01, p < 0.01).

mechanism_certainty.comment: Cross-sectional observational regression design (capped at <=2); rated 1 because the study documents statistical associations between tenure (home ownership), statutory utility service area jurisdictions (PCAs), and regulatory/utility indicators and household-reported supply interruptions using secondary data, without directly observing the administrative or legal mechanisms driving intermittency (and home ownership operated counter to the authors' hypothesised mechanism).

outcome_flags.comment: Primary outcome is household-reported piped water service continuity/intermittency (>=1 full day unavailable in past two weeks) alongside utility/regulator hours of supply per day (service_continuity, service_reliability); also analyses regulator/utility residential consumption in litres per capita per day against the 50 LPCD benchmark (service_quantity) and piped connection type across wealth groups (water_access).

sample_size.comment: 8,117 rural households in 347 clusters, 47 households in 2 clusters missing GPS coordinates, 1,574 households not drinking piped water, and 46 households answering 'don't know' on continuity were excluded to yield the analytic sample of 3,047 households in 177 clusters across all 11 Zambian WSCs; 54 African Union member states were screened in the preliminary secondary data audit.
sample_size.value: 3,047 urban and peri-urban households nested in 177 DHS household clusters across 11 commercial Water and Sewerage Companies (WSCs) / provider coverage areas (plus 54 African Union member states screened in preliminary data audit)

study_design.comment: Secondary cross-sectional spatial linkage and two-level multilevel logistic regression (households nested in DHS clusters, with provider fixed effects in Model 1 and provider-level covariates in Model 2), preceded by a systematic secondary data availability audit across 54 African Union member states.
study_design.value: Cross-sectional observational study spatially linking georeferenced household survey data (2018 Zambia DHS) with utility (2017 IBNET) and regulator (2018 NWASCO) records, analysed via two-level multilevel logistic regression
